title: Break-even analysis with a worked calculation for Post-construction clean
audience: Any post-construction cleaning operator who sets prices or plans monthly revenue, including solo operators whose work arrives in lumpy handover jobs.
learningOutcomes: Classify the costs of a post-construction cleaning business as fixed or variable
Calculate monthly break-even revenue from fixed costs and a variable cost percentage
Explain why conflicting break-even figures must be reconciled before any of them is used

instruction.heading: What break-even means
instruction.body: Break-even revenue is the amount of sales that covers all costs exactly, so profit is zero. Below that level the business loses money. Above it, each further dollar of sales adds to profit. Handover work arrives in lumps, tied to project completion dates, so a single month can look strong or empty. Break-even turns that uneven flow into a number of jobs you must complete each month. It is a planning tool, and its answer is only as good as the costs and percentages behind it.

instruction.heading: Split costs into fixed and variable
instruction.body: Fixed costs do not change with the number of jobs in a month. They include insurance, the vehicle, phone and software subscriptions, storage space, equipment hire and loan repayments. Variable costs move with each job. They include consumables and chemicals used on a handover, subcontracted labour and the card fees charged on each payment. Express variable cost as a percentage of sales: divide the variable cost in a period by the sales in the same period. ANZ defines the two cost types and warns that costs must be covered to avoid running at a loss (ANZ, 21 February 2025, last modified 22 July 2025). Check that percentage across at least three periods before relying on it, because a single busy or quiet month can mislead.

instruction.heading: The formula
instruction.body: Break-even revenue equals fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage. The quantity one minus the variable percentage is the contribution margin: the share of each dollar of sales that is left to cover fixed costs. Use the variable percentage as a decimal, so 15 per cent becomes 0.15. The contribution margin of a 15 per cent variable cost is 0.85.

instruction.heading: Work the calculation in order
instruction.body: Write the inputs first, each with its source and date. Then compute the contribution margin. Then divide the fixed costs by it. Finally convert the result into a number of jobs at your average job price, and round up to whole jobs, because a part job does not cover costs on its own. Xero's glossary gives a job count of 2.5 rounded up to 3 in practice (Xero Australia, 23 July 2026). Its example figures are for other businesses and are not used here. The research found no sourced average handover price, so your average must come from your own past jobs, recorded with its date.

instruction.heading: Reconcile before you use any figure
instruction.body: When two figures disagree, go back to the inputs. Confirm that each fixed cost is a monthly amount and not an annual one. Confirm that the variable percentage is a share of sales and not of cost. Confirm that the output is revenue and not profit. Then write down the reconciled figure with its inputs and drop the others. Do not borrow office or strata rates to fill a gap in your average job price, because the research found no post-construction benchmark to reconcile against.

procedure: List every monthly cost and label each one fixed or variable.
Work out variable cost as a percentage of sales for the same period, and check it across at least three months.
Calculate one minus the variable percentage to find the contribution margin.
Divide monthly fixed costs by the contribution margin to get break-even revenue.
Divide break-even revenue by your average job price from past jobs to get the number of jobs needed each month, rounded up.
Compare any other break-even figure with your result, reconcile the inputs, and keep only the reconciled figure.

workedExamples.situation: A two-person post-construction cleaning business (illustrative figures, with no market source) has fixed costs of $3,000 a month for insurance, the vehicle, software, storage and equipment hire, variable costs of 15 per cent of sales, and an average handover job price of $900 from its own past jobs (illustrative).
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How many handover jobs must the business complete each month to break even, and what should it check before using the $900 average?
workedExamples.reasoning: The contribution margin is 1 minus 0.15, which is 0.85. Break-even revenue is $3,000 divided by 0.85, which is $3,529.41 a month. Each job contributes $765 ($900 multiplied by 0.85) towards fixed costs. That is 3.92 jobs, so the business needs 4 jobs a month. Before using the $900, check that it is the average of your own recorded jobs after discounts, that the 15 per cent includes every per-job cost, and that the $3,000 is a monthly figure. No post-construction benchmark exists in the research to check the $900 against.

equipmentAndPpe: Cost list for the last three months

commonErrors.prevention: Convert every cost to the same period before dividing, and label each input with its period.

commonErrors.error: Using variable cost as a share of cost instead of a share of sales
commonErrors.prevention: Divide variable cost by sales for the same period, and write the denominator beside the percentage.

commonErrors.error: Copying a break-even figure from a plan without its inputs, or borrowing another trade's price
commonErrors.prevention: Recalculate from your own inputs and record the source and date of each input before using the result.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Business planning only. This lesson gives no tax or accounting advice. Check the tax treatment of costs, and GST on your prices, with a registered tax agent or qualified accountant. The ATO's page on GST registration sets a $75,000 GST turnover threshold (last updated 14 September 2026).

qualityStandard: Every break-even figure shows its fixed costs, variable percentage, period and source.
Two figures that disagree are reconciled before either one is used in a plan or a price.
documentationEvidence: Cost list split into fixed and variable, with source and date
Reconciliation note wherever two figures disagree
summary: Break-even revenue is fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage.
Use one period throughout the calculation.
Recalculate from your own inputs, including your own average job price. No post-construction benchmark was found.

knowledgeChecks.question: Break-even revenue is calculated as:
options: Fixed costs divided by (1 minus the variable cost percentage)
Fixed costs multiplied by the variable cost percentage
Sales minus fixed costs, shown as a percentage of the cost

knowledgeChecks.question: Fixed costs are $3,000 a month and variable costs are 15% of sales. What is the monthly break-even revenue?
Two sources give different break-even figures for the same business. What is the right response?
options: Use the larger figure to be safe and ignore the smaller figure entirely
Recalculate from your own costs and check each source's inputs before using any figure
Average the two figures together and quote the result to the builder today
Use the price list alone and skip the break-even check and rely on the owner's gut feel
